documents: Chang, Inoue, Misawa & Arai 2023, Architecture, formation and implication of active structure-controlled intraslope channel system southeast offshore Sendai, Tohoku, Japan. Basin Research 35:802-824 (published PDF)

entry.evidence: it remains unclear how CLTZs are influenced by active structures

sequences.source_document: Chang et al. 2023, Basin Research 35:802-824 (published PDF)

steps.action: The authors pose the open question of how channel-lobe transition zones and slope channels are influenced by active structures on active margins.
steps.quote: it remains unclear how CLTZs are influenced by active structures

steps.action: From existing bathymetry they identify and name an unnamed slope channel off Sendai, the Ishinomaki slope channel (ISC), between basement highs.
steps.quote: the bathymetric data southeast offshore Sendai shows that there is an unnamed slope channel

steps.action: They take from Baba & Yoshida (2020) the published location of a transform fault system of the Honjo-Sendai (Ishinomaki) tectonic line beneath the channel.
steps.quote: ISC appears to occur over a transform fault system of the Ishinomaki tectonic line

steps.action: They state the aim: describe the sedimentary and stratigraphic features of ISC and its CLTZ, and their structural and basement controls.
steps.quote: The objective of this study was to investigate the sedimentary and stratigraphic features of ISC and associated CLTZ

steps.action: They map bathymetry, free-air gravity and magnetic anomalies (public grids). They note a gravity low along ISC and a nearby magnetic low, which they read as a crustal-scale tectonic feature.
steps.quote: a local gravity anomaly low occurs approximately along ISC

steps.action: They select nine archived single-channel seismic reflection profiles from the 1980s (GSJ data bank): three across the upper domain, three across the lower domain and three along the channel axis.
steps.quote: we used seismic reflection profiles archived in the seismic data bank of the Geological Survey of Japan (GSJ)

steps.action: They adopt published models of intraslope basin and channel development from the literature: fill-and-spill, the two-phase model, and the Mitchell et al. (2021) structured-slope models (unstructured, diversion, deflection, confinement).
steps.quote: A two-phase model of submarine channel development, including early migration and later aggradation, is widely applied

steps.action: They state the expected signatures of each structured-slope model in thalweg trajectory and sinuosity, taken from Mitchell et al. (2021).
steps.quote: The model suggests that the structural influences are commonly distinct and can be recognized by the thalweg trajectory in the profile

steps.action: In the upper-domain profiles they interpret a half-channel-shaped composite basal surface, buried channels SSC01-SSC10, HARs, plugs and LAPs, together showing asymmetric northward thalweg migration.
steps.quote: the channel thalweg tends to migrate toward the north and the coeval depositional channel bank develops mostly on the southern side

steps.action: In the lower domain they observe normal faults that cut the channel fill and reach the seafloor as scarps, so the faults are active. They read discontinuous steep reflectors beneath the thalweg as high-angle strike-slip faults.
steps.quote: these normal faults crop out and form seafloor fault scarps

steps.action: They check the basal surface and individual channel surfaces by correlating them between cross-channel and dip profiles, over more than 10 km.
steps.quote: Based on lateral examination of the seismic reflection profiles in different orientations, we found that this surface can be correlated

steps.action: They propose that ISC formed by convergence between the active, northward-migrating Abukuma ridge and the inactive South Kitakami massif. Evidence: faulted southern flank, unfaulted thin cover on the northern promontory.
steps.quote: we suggest that the formation of ISC is the result of convergence between the active, northward-migrating Abukuma ridge

steps.action: They compare the observed oblique stacking and thalweg trajectory with the Mitchell et al. (2021) model cases and find the closest match in local confinement on negative relief (Figure 4c4).
steps.quote: Both the channel stacking pattern and obliquely stacked thalweg trajectory are mostly similar to the cases

steps.action: From growth-strata-like fanning and from contact angles between fill and basal surface, they infer rapid fault-controlled subsidence upstream, limited subsidence downstream, and therefore differential subsidence along the trough.
steps.quote: We conclude that the great and limited subsidence in the upper and lower domains indicates differential subsidence

steps.action: They keep the claim that ISC is a structure-dominated intraslope channel confined by active basement structures, with a fault trough as its prototype.
steps.quote: ISC is affected by active structural confinement

steps.action: For the wave-like seafloor features at the channel mouth they list rival origins: gullies, sediment waves, contourites, or structural features.
steps.quote: are gullies, sediment waves, contourite deposits or structural features may be an issue to clarify

steps.action: They exclude gullies (these favour steeper slopes, not a slope break) and faults (no fault seen beneath the features).
steps.quote: gullies and faults interpretations can be excluded

steps.action: They compare the wavelength and height of the features (ca. 1 km, ca. 150 m) with published sediment waves (Valencia margin, Azores) and with contourites.
steps.quote: is a little bit greater than those of the sediment waves on the Valencia margin

steps.action: They tentatively keep sediment waves and channel-mouth lobes, which together indicate a CLTZ, and conclude that the CLTZ is structure-controlled by the bounding basement structures.
steps.quote: it is clear that the CLTZ of ISC is structure-controlled

steps.action: They explain the coexisting shallow listric faults, the reverse and normal faults and the deep strike-slip faults by a releasing bend on the strike-slip Honjo-Sendai tectonic line (after Sanchez et al. 2010). They deduce a former united Kitakami-Abukuma ridge.
steps.quote: Here, we ascribe these structural features to the nature of the strike-slip Honjo-Sendai tectonic line.

steps.action: They assemble a five-stage simplified tectonic and sedimentary evolution model (Figure 9): a united ridge, strike-slip splitting into a fault trough, channelization, migration, and filled-overfilled basin.
steps.quote: a simplified tectonic and sedimentary evolution model for ISC is proposed here

steps.action: They propose that sediment trapped in the filled-overfilled intraslope basin explains the smaller 2011 event-deposit volume in the central Japan Trench reported by Kioka et al. (2019).
steps.quote: provides a supportive source-to-sink interpretation of the unexplained volume difference of the extreme event sediments

steps.action: They conclude that ISC is active structure-controlled, likely by the strike-slip Honjo-Sendai tectonic line, with differential subsidence. They propose a former Kitakami-Abukuma ridge and suggest the basin and CLTZ may preserve records of extreme events.
steps.quote: we propose that there was a basement rock (Kitakami-Abukuma ridge)

tree.answer: A structure-controlled intraslope channel, its CLTZ and the underlying basin off Sendai
Partly: seafloor morphology directly; buried architecture only through archived single-channel seismic profiles
Describe the architecture and infer the structural controls and evolution
Yes: published channel-structure models (unstructured, diversion, deflection, confinement); for the seafloor waves, gullies, contourites, faults or sediment waves
Yes, qualitatively: thalweg trajectory and stacking differ among models; bedform dimensions differ between sediment waves and contourites
Found, not set: a past and ongoing structural history read from traces

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Weakly: repeated profiles across the same channel, not independent events
Only consistency of surfaces across profiles of different orientation; no sensitivity tests or independent data
Kept as best explanation; CLTZ interpretation tentative; former ridge a deduction
Not assessed: review history only linked, not supplied

end.claim: The Ishinomaki slope channel and its CLTZ are confined and controlled by active basement structures (an active Abukuma ridge to the south, the stable South Kitakami massif to the north), most likely through the strike-slip Honjo-Sendai tectonic line with differential subsidence.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the interpretation of the archived seismic profiles (basal surface, obliquely stacked buried channels, and faults cutting the fill and seafloor), there would be no claim of an active structure-controlled channel.

gates.evidence: The seismic data were collected in the early 1980s for marine geological mapping, not for this hypothesis (p. 808). The structural reading was compared with published model cases (p. 815). Rival origins of the seafloor waves were excluded on slope position, the absence of underlying faults, and dimensions (p. 816). The headline claim and the Kitakami-Abukuma ridge, however, are interpretive deductions without a stated test that could fail (p. 817 calls the ridge "a rational deduction"). Nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: Hydraulic jump and the supercritical/subcritical flow transition, used to characterize CLTZs and turbidity currents

novelty_claims.quote: the role previously unrecognized ISC may play in the sediment routing system of the central Japan Trench may require [...]
these interpretations and associated kinematics may provide a new scenario for the regional basement structure
there is an unnamed slope channel (referred to in this work as the Ishinomaki slope channel, or [...] )

limits: No peer-review file was supplied (the history is only linked at Publons, p. 820), so no review sequence is coded. The data are not public (p. 820). The single-channel profiles cannot image deeper structure beneath seafloor multiples (p. 809). No cores, wells or age control date the channel stages, so the evolution model (Figure 9) has no chronology. Sub-claims at other statuses: the CLTZ and sediment-wave interpretation is called tentative (best_explanation, p. 816). The former Kitakami-Abukuma ridge is a deduction and the authors call for direct observation (best_explanation at most, p. 817). The role of the basin and CLTZ as preservers of extreme-event deposits and the explanation of the Kioka et al. (2019) volume difference are untested implications (none, pp. 818-819). Inference: the criteria for choosing the nine profiles are not stated. Coding the cross-profile correlation as a V replication is a coder judgment: the profiles come from the same survey.

disagreements.target: Kioka et al. (2019): smaller event-sediment volume in the central Japan Trench attributed to the absence of a submarine canyon conduit
disagreements.support: The paper identifies a slope channel feeding a filled-overfilled intraslope basin that can trap sediment, and offers this as an alternative account of the volume difference.
disagreements.quote: there is at least one slope channel that is able to transport sediment downstream than it has been expected

disagreements.target: View that, lacking an underfilled forearc basin, Tohoku slope sediments discharge directly to the trench
disagreements.support: An intraslope basin beneath ISC and the CLTZ is shown as sediment storage, alongside the previously reported isolated basins.
disagreements.quote: the absence of the manifest underfilled forearc basin appears to imply that most island arc and

disagreements.target: Common position that CLTZs are sediment bypass zones of doubtful storage value
disagreements.support: Sediment waves and lobes are interpreted in this CLTZ, and preserved ancient CLTZs are cited, to argue that CLTZs are depositional elements.
disagreements.quote: CLTZs are generally considered to be a sediment bypass zones

alternatives_considered.reason: The head lies at about 150 m, slightly shallower than the shelfbreak, with no present-day river connection

alternatives_considered.chosen: High-angle strike-slip faults beneath the thalweg
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Fault with recognizable hanging wall and downthrown side (dip-slip)
alternatives_considered.reason: No clear hanging or downthrown side; steep and opposite-dipping reflectors

alternatives_considered.chosen: Channel on coeval-negative bathymetry, local confinement (Mitchell et al. 2021, Figure 4c4)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Unstructured slope (two-phase model); pre-structural diversion; coeval-positive deflection
alternatives_considered.reason: The channel stacking pattern and obliquely stacked thalweg trajectory are most similar to the c4 case

alternatives_considered.chosen: Sediment waves formed by outward spreading of channelized flow at the slope break
alternatives_considered.reason: Gullies favour steeper slopes; no fault lies beneath the features; the dimensions match sediment waves rather than contourites
